topics.name: -ly adverbs of manner and their comparison
Rhetorical questions: interrogative and assertive sentences
Linking words: though, although, despite, hardly ... when

options: The children laughed merrily at the joke.
The children laughs merrily at the joke.
The children laughed merry at the joke.
questions.rule: Merrily is an adverb telling how they laughed, and plural children takes laughed, not laughs.

options: If it will rain, the roses will bloom.
If it rains, the roses bloomed.
If it rains, the roses will bloom.
questions.rule: Type 1 conditional: if + simple present, then will + verb: If it rains, the roses will bloom.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: To say how she solved it, use the adverb cleverly, not the adjective clever.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Although needs a clause (subject + verb). Before a noun phrase like the heavy rain, use despite.
The word describes how to enjoy (a verb), so use the -ly adverb cheerfully.

questions.before: If you water the plants daily, they
questions.rule: For a general truth, use the simple present in both parts: If you water ..., they grow well.
In a wh-question the helping verb comes before the subject: Why should we ...?

chat: How did Kabir play in the final?
options: He played brilliant and scored fifty.
He played brilliantly and scored fifty.
He plays brilliantly and score fifty.
questions.rule: How did he play? needs an adverb: brilliantly. The question is in the past, so use played and scored.

questions.source: Who does not love a sunny morning?
options: Everyone does not love a sunny morning.
questions.rule: The question means that all people love it. So the statement is Everyone loves a sunny morning.
Nobody can becomes the rhetorical question Who can ...? It keeps the same meaning.

options: Though she was tired, but she helped her mother.
Despite she was tired, she helped her mother.
Though she was tired, she helped her mother.
questions.rule: Do not use but after though. Despite cannot take a clause like she was tired.

options: If I have wings, I would fly over the hills.
If I had wings, I will fly over the hills.
If I had wings, I would fly over the hills.
questions.rule: Type 2 (imagined) conditional: if + past, then would + verb: If I had wings, I would fly.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: The word tells how they marched, so use the adverb bravely.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: After will use the base form of the verb: will cancel.

questions.after: the dark clouds, the children kept playing in the park.
questions.rule: Despite is followed by a noun phrase (the dark clouds). Although needs a subject and verb.

questions.after: you, I would not lose hope.
questions.rule: For an imagined situation, use If I were you with would in the main clause.
Type 1: If + simple present, then will + verb: If you practise daily, your game will improve.

chat: Will you go to the park if it rains?
options: No, if it rains, I will stay at home.
No, if it will rain, I stay at home.
No, if it rained, I will staying at home.
questions.rule: Type 1 conditional: if it rains (simple present), I will stay (will + base verb).

options: Yes, although it rained, we had fun.
Yes, despite it rained, we had fun.
Yes, although it rained, but we had fun.
questions.rule: Although joins a clause and needs no but. Despite cannot be followed by it rained.

questions.source: Tara runs the fastest in her class.
options: Tara runs faster than any student in her class.
Tara runs more fast than any other student in her class.
Tara runs faster than any other student in her class.
questions.rule: Superlative to comparative: faster than any other. Without other, Tara would be compared with herself.
After linking verbs like smell, look, feel, use an adjective: smell sweet. Plural flowers takes smell.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Type 3 conditional: would have + past participle: would have caught.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Despite cannot introduce a clause (he smiled). Join the two contrasting clauses with but.
Comparing with all the climbers needs the superlative adverb: most fearlessly.

questions.before: If she had known about the test, she
questions.rule: Type 3 (past, unreal): if + had + past participle, then would have + past participle.
Despite + noun phrase (heavy rain), then the main clause: our team won the match.

chat: Why did you miss the bus?
options: If I had woke up earlier, I would not have missed it.
If I had woken up earlier, I would not have missed it.
If I had woken up earlier, I will not miss it.
questions.rule: Type 3: had woken (past participle) + would not have missed. Woke is the simple past, not the participle.

chat: I failed one test. I'm so upset.
options: Why losing hope over one test? You will do better next time.
Why lose hope over one test? You will doing better next time.
Why lose hope over one test? You will do better next time.
questions.rule: A short rhetorical question can be Why + base verb: Why lose hope? After will, use do.

questions.source: Can fear ever defeat true courage?
options: Fear can ever defeat true courage.
Fear could never defeated true courage.
Fear can never defeat true courage.
questions.rule: The question expects the answer 'No', so Can ... ever becomes can never, followed by the base verb.

questions.prompt: Find and fix the 2 errors in this message.
questions.rule: Both words tell how they did the action, so use adverbs: guard our goal carefully, passed the ball wisely.

options: Yesterday the boys play noisily in the rain.
Yesterday the boys played noisily in the rain.
Yesterday the boys played noisy in the rain.
questions.rule: Yesterday needs the past (played), and noisily is the adverb telling how they played.

options: Although each of the girls were tired, they finished the trek.
Although each of the girls was tired, they finished the trek.
Despite each of the girls was tired, they finished the trek.
questions.rule: Each of takes a singular verb (was). Although, not despite, introduces a clause.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: A word describing an adjective (high) must be an adverb: dangerously high.
The pair is hardly ... when. (No sooner goes with than.)
Unless means 'if not'. It takes the simple present (we leave), and the main clause uses will.

options: Not yet, but I will finished it quickly after dinner.
Not yet, but I will finish it quickly after dinner.
Not yet, but I finishing it quickly after dinner.
questions.rule: Use will + base verb for a future plan: I will finish it quickly. Quickly tells how.

options: We can't, as it is raining heavy. Let's play chess instead.
We can't, as it is raining heavily. Let's play chess instead.
We can't, as it raining heavily. Let's play chess instead.
questions.rule: Present continuous needs is: it is raining. The adverb heavily tells how it is raining.

questions.source: If you do not water the roses, they will not bloom.
options: Unless you water the roses, they will not bloom.
Unless you do not water the roses, they will not bloom.
Unless you water the roses, they will bloom.
questions.rule: Unless already means 'if not', so drop do not from the if-clause and keep the main clause the same.

questions.source: Although the hike was difficult, the friends kept going.
options: Despite the hike was difficult, the friends kept going.
Despite of the difficult hike, the friends kept going.
Despite the difficult hike, the friends kept going.
questions.rule: Despite takes a noun phrase (the difficult hike) and is never followed by of.

questions.prompt: Find and fix the 2 errors in this message.
questions.rule: The story is about last Sunday, so use the past: enjoyed. Held her hand needs the adverb carefully.

options: Had I known about the storm, I would stay at home yesterday.
Had I knew about the storm, I would have stayed at home.
Had I known about the storm, I would have stayed at home.
questions.rule: Had I known = If I had known (type 3). The main clause needs would have + past participle.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: No sooner is always paired with than: No sooner had ... than ...

questions.before: If the shower had not come, the roses
questions.rule: Type 3: if + had not come, then would not have bloomed for an unreal past result.
Had you told me = If you had told me. Then I would have helped (type 3).

chat: Why didn't Arjun come to the match?
options: He will have come if he had not been ill.
He would have come if he had not been ill.
He would have come if he has not been ill.
questions.rule: For an unreal past, pair would have come with if he had not been (type 3).

questions.source: As soon as the sun came out, the children ran outside.
options: No sooner did the sun come out than the children ran outside.
No sooner did the sun came out than the children ran outside.
No sooner did the sun come out when the children ran outside.
questions.rule: No sooner did + subject + base verb ... than. After did use come, and pair it with than.

questions.prompt: Change into a negative sentence without changing the meaning.
options: Hope does not always rise again.
Hope never fails to rise again.
Hope never fail to rise again.
questions.rule: always rises = never fails to rise. Singular Hope takes fails.

questions.prompt: Find and fix the 3 errors in this message.
questions.rule: cut bamboo tirelessly (adverb); helped him (object pronoun); would never have built (past participle).

questions.prompt: Find and fix the 2 errors in this message.
questions.rule: If I were (imagined) pairs with would fly. With the plural subject My friends and I, the verb has no -s: enjoy.

questions.prompt: Find and fix the 3 errors in this message.
questions.rule: After does not use the base verb love; too much rain spoils and every farmer worries take singular verbs.
